question: Was Kabīr a disciple of Rāmānanda?

sides.position: Yes: Kabīr was one of Rāmānanda's twelve disciples; lying on the steps of the Pañcagaṅgā ghāṭ he received the Name 'Rām' when Rāmānanda stepped on him; his Rām is Rāmānanda's.
arguments: the Rāmānandī hagiographies (Anantadās, Nābhādās) say so
the popular line 'kāśī meṃ ham pragaṭ bhae, rāmānand ceṭāe' (late, of doubtful authenticity)

sides.position: No human guru was needed: Kabīr is the Sat Puruṣ incarnate who came in every age; he accepted Rāmānanda outwardly only to establish the custom of taking a guru (some panth accounts even make Rāmānanda his disciple).
arguments: Kabīr appeared on a lotus and was not born of a womb
the Satguru of Kabīr's songs is the Lord, not a man

historical_debates.name: Hagiographical claims
historical_debates.accounts: Anantadās's Kabīr Paracaī and Nābhādās's Bhaktamāl vs the Kabīr Panth literature

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: a question of lineage fact on which the two traditions' accounts differ.
candidate_readings: P6-upaya: the Kabīr Panth's own reading — Kabīr modelled discipleship as a skilful means; rejected by Rāmānandīs, who hold the discipleship real
P2-standpoint: outward initiation by Rāmānanda (social standpoint) and the inner satguru (the Lord) are both affirmed; rejected by the Kabīr Panth insofar as it makes Kabīr a disciple
Scholarly chronology (metadata only): Rāmānanda's traditional dates (c. 1299–1410) make direct discipleship difficult for a Kabīr of c. 1440–1518
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kabīr Panth rejects any account that subordinates Kabīr; the Rāmānandīs reject the claim that Kabīr needed no guru.

question: Is the Rām of the Sants the avatāra, Rāma son of Daśaratha?

sides.position: No: 'the son of Daśaratha is praised in the three worlds, but the secret of Rām's name is other'; Rām is the unborn Lord in every body.
arguments: Rām pervades every body (musk in the deer)
what is born and dies is not the Lord

sides.position: The avatāras come from the regions of Kāl to keep order; the Saints come from the highest region; the Saints are above the avatāras.
arguments: the avatāras do not take souls beyond the three worlds

sides.position: Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheś are Kāl's sons; Kabīr, not the avatāras, frees souls.
Yes: the one whom the Vedas sing and sages meditate on is the son of Daśaratha, lord of Kosala, for the sake of his devotees; there is no difference between saguṇa and nirguṇa.
arguments: the formless takes form out of love for devotees

reconciliation.explanation: Under P3-path the same Rām is approached through the Name within (Sants) and through the avatāra's form (Rāmānandīs); Tulsīdās's own 'no difference between saguṇa and nirguṇa' supports this from the saguṇa side.
reconciliation.detail: The reconciliation claims only that both paths address one Lord; it does not claim the Sants accept the avatāra as supreme.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kabīr Panth and Sant Mat reject equality: for them the avatāras belong to Kāl's domain. The Rāmānandīs reject any view that makes Rāma less than the supreme Brahman.

notes: A special case of dsp:saguna-nirguna (owned by U50).

question: Is Nirañjan the stainless supreme or a lower, deceiving power (Kāl)?

sides.position: Alakh Nirañjan, the stainless unseen, is the ultimate of the yogīs.
Nirañjan is the formless stainless Lord, object of devotion and yoga.
Dādū bows first to Nirañjan in his Vāṇī.
Nirañjan is Kāl, the fallen son of the Sat Puruṣ, creator and jailer of the three worlds.
arguments: he won the worlds by austerity and swallowed Ādyā

sides.position: Jot Nirañjan rules the first region (Sahasdal Kanwal) and belongs to Kāl's domain; those who stop there take a lower lord for the highest.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the same name is the highest for some lineages and a lower power for others.
candidate_readings: P4-stage: Sant Mat's own reading — those who reached only the first region named its lord supreme; rejected by Nāths and Nirañjanīs
P1-level: nirañjana as the absolute (stainless) vs Nirañjan as the ruler of the created worlds (cosmic function); rejected by the Kabīr Panth, for whom Kāl is not the Sat Puruṣ in any aspect

Homonymy: the name denotes different things in different lineages (so no single question); weakened if, as some scholars suggest, the Kabīr Panth myth deliberately answers the Nāth/Nirañjanī theology (scholarly suggestion, metadata only)
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each side insists on its own valuation of the name.

question: What place, if any, has yogic discipline (haṭha, aṣṭāṅga, kuṇḍalinī) on the Sant path of the Name?

sides.position: None as a means: sahaj is best — no closing of eyes, stopping of ears or mortification; the yogī dyes his clothes, not his mind; the Name and love suffice.
arguments: forced yoga breeds pride and display
the Lord is found by love and the Name

sides.position: Sundardās teaches aṣṭāṅga and haṭha yoga (postures, breath, cakras, the serpent power) as a stage within the Sant path, below devotion and knowledge.
Caraṇdās teaches the eight limbs of yoga to his disciples as a support of devotion to Kṛṣṇa and the guru.
Only the yoga of the sound current, beginning at the eye centre, is needed; haṭha and kuṇḍalinī work on the lower centres is unnecessary and hazardous; surat-śabd yoga is the crown of yogas.

reconciliation.explanation: Sundardās and Caraṇdās themselves place yoga as a preparatory stage (P4) under the Name and devotion; temperaments differ (P3).
reconciliation.detail: Claims only that the Sant tradition contains this graded view; it does not claim that Kabīr's verses or Sant Mat accept yoga as a stage.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Kabīr's verses reject forced yoga outright; Sant Mat rejects lower-centre yoga as unnecessary; for the Nāth side of the wider question see dsp:kabir-and-the-yogis (U21).

notes: Intra-Sant counterpart of dsp:kabir-and-the-yogis (U21, Nāth vs Sant), which records the Kabīr–Gorakh goṣṭhī.

question: Is the Sahajiyā path (and those of the Bāuls and Kartābhajās) a true form of Caitanya's Vaiṣṇavism?

sides.position: Yes: Caitanya (Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in one body) and the Gosvāmīs taught the sahaja doctrine esoterically; the Caitanya-caritāmṛta has an inner Sahajiyā meaning; parakīyā love is to be realized by human partners who see each other as Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā, turning kāma into prema.
arguments: the kāma/prema distinction requires transformation, not suppression
rūpa and svarūpa: the divine couple are in every human pair

sides.position: No: parakīyā belongs only to Kṛṣṇa's līlā and may never be imitated by humans; kāma (desire for one's own pleasure) and prema (desire for Kṛṣṇa's) are opposites; the Gosvāmīs were strict renunciants. Later orthodoxy lists Āul, Bāul, Kartābhajā, Neḍā, Daraveś, Sāṃi, Sahajiyā, Sakhībhekī, Smārta, Jāt-gosāñi, Ativāḍī, Cūḍādhārī and Gaurāṅga-nāgarī as deviant sects (apasampradāya).
arguments: imitating the līlā is an offence
Rūpa Kavirāja's abandonment of vaidhī rules was condemned (18th c.)

sides.position: Caitanya himself returned as Āulcānd to reveal the secret sahaja religion to the poor; outward conformity hides the true teaching.

historical_debates.name: Condemnation of Rūpa Kavirāja
historical_debates.accounts: Gauḍīya accounts of Viśvanātha Cakravartin's refutation (low confidence on details)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Rūpa Kavirāja excluded by the orthodox

historical_debates.name: The apasampradāya lists
historical_debates.accounts: Gauḍīya Maṭh literature (the list of thirteen deviant groups is commonly attributed to Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura; moderate confidence)

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: each side rejects the other's reading of the same Caitanya literature.
candidate_readings: P1-level: parakīyā true of the divine līlā but not of human conduct — this is the orthodox position itself and is rejected by the Sahajiyā
P5-neyartha: the Sahajiyā reading of the Caitanya-caritāmṛta as the definitive (nītārtha) meaning behind a provisional surface — the Sahajiyā's own hermeneutic, rejected by the Gauḍīyas
P3-path / P4-stage: different qualifications (adhikāra) for different practitioners — rejected by the orthodox as licensing transgression
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Gauḍīya orthodoxy regards the Sahajiyā practice as a fall into kāma; the Sahajiyā regards orthodox practice as external (bāhya) and preliminary.

notes: Related: dsp:svakiya-parakiya (U16, internal Gauḍīya debate on the divine līlā).

question: Is a living master necessary, and how is the true successor known?

sides.position: A living Sant Satguru is indispensable; each master designates his successor; Jaimal Singh was authorized by Soamiji to initiate in the Punjab, and the Beas line continues by designation.
arguments: past masters cannot initiate or guide the living

sides.position: The Agra lines trace the true succession through Soamiji's own circle (Rai Salig Ram and after, or Soamiji's family at Soamibagh, or the Dayalbagh line) and have not accepted the other lines' claims.
The Dharamdāsī Kabīr Panth locates authority in a hereditary line of forty-two ācāryas promised by Kabīr, not in spiritual designation.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: each line claims the true succession.
candidate_readings: P4-stage / P3-path: different lines serving different disciples — rejected by each line as denying the uniqueness of the true master
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Each line holds that the true master is one.

notes: Details of the Agra lines' positions are recalled with low confidence.

question: Was Kabīr a Hindu or a Muslim?

sides.position: A Vaiṣṇava devotee of Rām and disciple of Rāmānanda.

Neither: the Sat Puruṣ appeared as a child on a lotus at Lahartārā and was raised by the Muslim weavers Nīrū and Nīmā; at his death only flowers were found, divided for a samādhi and a tomb at Maghar.
Kabīr's own verses disown both: Hindu and Turk fight over Rām and Rahīm and neither knows the secret.

historical_debates.name: The dispute over Kabīr's body at Maghar
historical_debates.accounts: Kabīr Panth and popular hagiography; Maghar has both a samādhi and a mazār

reconciliation.explanation: Under P2, 'Muslim weaver' (by upbringing), 'devotee of Rām' (by devotion) and 'neither' (by his own teaching) are statements from different standpoints.
reconciliation.detail: Claims only that the accounts answer different questions; it does not settle the hagiographic facts.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kabīr Panth rejects a human birth; the Rāmānandīs reject 'neither'; Muslim claims (e.g. Kabīr as a Sufi pīr) are outside this ontology's scope and recorded only as context.
